title: Bengaluru AI Firm and Mayo Clinic Target Undruggable Pancreatic Cancer Protein With New Drug Candidate
excerpt: Sravathi AI helped screen nearly 40,000 compounds to find a molecule that blocks the GIPC1 protein, slowing tumor growth in preclinical studies published in Cell Reports.
body:
• Bengaluru-based Sravathi AI and Mayo Clinic developed a first-in-class small molecule that blocks the PDZ domain of the GIPC1 protein, a target previously considered undruggable.
  • AI-driven screening of nearly 40,000 compounds identified the candidate, which slowed pancreatic tumor growth and improved survival in laboratory studies.
  • The drug enhanced the effects of gemcitabine, a standard chemotherapy, and showed signs of altering the tumor microenvironment.
  • The findings, published in Cell Reports, remain preclinical — no human testing has been announced.

An AI-Powered Drug Discovery Breakthrough

Mayo Clinic researchers, working with Bengaluru-based Sravathi AI Technology for IP Sharing, have used artificial intelligence to develop an experimental drug that targets a protein region long considered impossible to hit with conventional medicines. The compound, termed GIPCi, blocks the PDZ domain of the GIPC1 protein — a scaffolding molecule that helps pancreatic cancer cells grow, survive, and resist treatment.

The findings, published in Cell Reports on July 31, represent a rare example of AI-assisted drug discovery reaching the preclinical validation stage for one of the deadliest forms of cancer. Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma has a five-year survival rate below 13 percent, largely because tumors are typically diagnosed late and rapidly develop resistance to available therapies.

"Our study demonstrates that AI can help us identify entirely new therapeutic opportunities against targets that have historically been considered undruggable. While these findings are preclinical, they provide a strong foundation for the next phase of research."

— Debabrata (Dev) Mukhopadhyay, Ph.D., Senior Author, Mayo Clinic

How the AI Screening Worked

GIPC1 functions as a molecular scaffold, organizing signaling networks that cancer cells exploit to proliferate and evade therapy. Its PDZ domain — a structural region involved in protein-protein interactions — presents a broad, shallow binding surface that conventional drug design has historically struggled to target.

The research team used Sravathi AI's computational platform to screen nearly 40,000 potential compounds before identifying one capable of blocking the GIPC1 PDZ domain. Rather than targeting obvious catalytic sites, the AI-driven approach focused on disrupting the structural interactions that help cancer cells coordinate their signaling machinery.

In laboratory studies, the experimental drug slowed tumor growth and improved survival in mouse models. Critically, it also enhanced the effects of gemcitabine, a frontline chemotherapy for pancreatic cancer, producing better outcomes than either treatment alone.

Changing the Tumor Environment

Beyond directly inhibiting GIPC1, the compound showed early signs of altering the tumor microenvironment — the protective ecosystem that surrounds pancreatic tumors and helps them resist treatment. These changes could open the door to future combination therapies, according to the researchers.

The work also demonstrates how AI can accelerate the timeline for identifying drug candidates against difficult targets. Traditional screening methods for protein-protein interaction inhibitors are notoriously slow and expensive. Sravathi AI's platform compressed this process significantly, identifying viable candidates from tens of thousands of possibilities.

A Bengaluru Connection to Frontier Medicine

Sravathi AI, based in Bangalore, India, specializes in AI-driven intellectual property and drug discovery platforms. The collaboration with Mayo Clinic highlights the growing role of Indian AI firms in global pharmaceutical research, particularly in targeting diseases that have resisted conventional drug development approaches.

The partnership is part of a broader trend of cross-border collaborations leveraging India's AI talent pool for frontier biomedical applications, from drug discovery to diagnostics.

What Comes Next

The researchers emphasized that the therapy remains experimental. No human testing has been announced, and additional studies will be needed to evaluate safety and determine whether the compound can advance to clinical trials. The team is exploring whether GIPC1 inhibition could also be effective against other cancers where the protein is overexpressed.

If the compound eventually reaches clinical development, it would represent a milestone in AI-assisted oncology — proof that machine learning can unlock drug targets that decades of conventional research left untouched.
